11250:
Obscurity means the state of being hidden from attention — either because something is unknown, unclear, or dark. Think of it as the opposite of being in a spotlight. Whatever is in obscurity is somewhere in the shadows — unseen, unheard of, or hard to make sense of.

The word has three distinct but closely related meanings. Understanding all three will give you complete command of it.

This is the most common use of the word. When a person, place, or thing is in obscurity, it means nobody knows about it, or very few people do. It exists, but the world hasn't noticed.

Examples:

  • "The artist spent most of his life in obscurity, painting in a tiny village that no one visited."
  • "After her one hit song, she faded back into obscurity."
  • "The town remained in obscurity until a famous movie was filmed there."

In all these cases, obscurity is about being invisible to the world — not literally invisible, but socially and publicly invisible. No fame, no recognition, no spotlight.

This sense of the word often carries a slightly sad feeling. To rise from obscurity is seen as a triumph. To sink into obscurity is often seen as a kind of failure or loss.

Key idea: If something is in obscurity, the world doesn't know it exists — or has completely forgotten that it does.

Here, obscurity refers to lack of clarity — in writing, speech, ideas, or meaning. When something is described as having "obscurity," it means it is confusing, vague, or hard to figure out. The meaning is hidden, as if in a fog.

Examples:

  • "The philosopher's writing was full of obscurity — even scholars struggled to understand what he meant."
  • "The obscurity of the tax law made it nearly impossible for ordinary people to follow."
  • "Her poem had a deliberate obscurity to it — she wanted readers to think hard about what it meant."

In this sense, obscurity isn't about fame or recognition — it's about comprehension. If a text has obscurity, you have to work hard to understand it. Sometimes this is accidental (the writer was careless or unclear). Other times it is intentional (the writer wanted to be mysterious or complex).

Key idea: If a piece of writing or an idea has obscurity, its meaning is buried — it doesn't come through clearly.

This is the oldest and least common use today. In literature and formal writing, obscurity can refer to actual darkness, shadow, or the condition of being physically hidden from sight.

Examples:

  • "The old castle disappeared into the obscurity of the night."
  • "He moved through the obscurity of the fog, invisible to those around him."

You won't encounter this meaning much in everyday conversation, but you will see it in novels, poetry, and older writing. It connects neatly with the other meanings because in all cases — whether unknown, unclear, or physically dark — the idea of being hidden or unseen runs through the word.

The word can also be used in plural — obscurities — to refer to specific unclear or confusing parts of something.

Example:

  • "The editor asked the author to fix the obscurities in chapter three — certain passages just didn't make sense."

Here, "obscurities" means specific moments of confusion rather than a general quality.
How Obscurity Feels in a Sentence

The word can refer to a state, a quality, or a degree:

  • A state: "He lived in obscurity." (He was unknown.)
  • A quality: "The obscurity of the contract confused the buyers." (The contract was unclear.)
  • With degree: "The instructions were written with such obscurity that no one could follow them." (A high degree of unclarity.)

To sharpen your understanding, here is what stands opposite to obscurity:

  • The opposite of obscurity (being unknown) is fame, prominence, renown, or recognition.
  • The opposite of obscurity (being unclear) is clarity, lucidity, or transparency.

Picture a room with no lights on. You are standing in it. You cannot see anything clearly. You don't know what's in the corners. Things exist in that room, but they are hidden from you. That room is a perfect image of obscurity — things hidden, unseen, unknown, and unclear.

Whether a person is forgotten by the world, a piece of writing is too confusing to follow, or something is literally swallowed up by darkness — all of it is obscurity.
11251:
Obsequies means the formal ceremonies and rituals performed for a person who has died — in other words, a funeral in its full, ceremonial sense. Think of it as everything that is officially and solemnly done to honor a dead person and see them off: the service, the prayers, the procession, the burial or cremation rites. All of that, taken together, is the "obsequies."

If someone says "the obsequies were held on Friday," they are simply saying that the funeral ceremonies took place on Friday.
Important: It Is Almost Always Plural

This is a crucial point. You will almost never see the singular "obsequy" in real use. The word naturally appears in its plural form — obsequies — because a funeral is not one single act but a collection of ceremonial acts performed together. Just as we say "proceedings" rather than "a proceeding" when referring to a series of formal actions, we say "obsequies" to capture the full bundle of funeral rituals.

When people use the word "obsequies," they are typically referring to the entire ceremonial experience surrounding a person's death and burial. This can include:

  • The formal funeral service (prayers, eulogies, readings)
  • The procession of mourners
  • The burial or cremation ceremony
  • Any solemn religious or traditional rites performed for the deceased

It is the whole dignified, ceremonial affair — not just a quick, informal goodbye, but a structured, formal send-off with proper ritual and gravity.
The Tone and Register of This Word

This is not an everyday word. It is formal, literary, and somewhat elevated in tone. You would not hear someone say "I'm heading to John's obsequies" in casual conversation — they would say "funeral" instead. "Obsequies" tends to appear in:

  • Literature, poetry, and historical writing
  • Formal announcements or obituaries
  • Religious or ceremonial contexts
  • Journalism when describing the funeral of a prominent person

The word carries a sense of solemnity and dignity. When a writer chooses "obsequies" over "funeral," they are deliberately giving the event a grander, more ceremonial weight. It signals that this was not just a death, but a formal, meaningful human ritual of farewell.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Funeral is the everyday, neutral word most people use. It refers to the event broadly.

Obsequies is the formal, elevated version of the same idea, but with a stronger emphasis on the ceremonial and ritual dimension. It highlights the rites and observances being performed, not just the event as a social gathering.

Last rites refers specifically to religious sacraments administered to a person who is dying or has just died (especially in Catholicism). Obsequies, by contrast, refer to what happens after death — the broader set of funeral ceremonies.

Burial refers only to the act of placing the body in the ground. Obsequies are far broader than this — they include everything surrounding that moment.

• "The king's obsequies lasted three days, attended by dignitaries from across the world."
  • "She sat quietly through the obsequies, too grief-stricken to speak."
  • "The general's obsequies were conducted with full military honors."
  • "After the obsequies, the family gathered at the home for a meal."

Notice how in each case, the word points to the formal, ceremonial proceedings of a funeral — and how it lends the sentence a slightly elevated, dignified tone.
The One Thing to Always Remember

If you want to lock this word in your memory forever, hold onto this idea:

Obsequies = the solemn, formal ceremonies performed to honor and bury the dead.

It is essentially a grand, formal word for a funeral's ceremonial proceedings. Whenever you see it, picture the full, dignified ritual of a funeral — the prayers, the procession, the rites — all of it wrapped into one word.
11252:
Imagine someone who constantly agrees with their boss, laughs at every one of their jokes (even the bad ones), rushes to fetch their coffee before being asked, and showers them with compliments like "That's such a brilliant idea!" — even when it isn't. This person isn't being genuinely kind or respectful. They're performing kindness to gain something: a promotion, approval, or simply to avoid getting into trouble.

That behaviour — being excessively eager to please someone, especially someone powerful, in a way that feels fake, overly submissive, and self-serving — is what the adjective obsequious describes.

There are three things happening at once when you call someone obsequious:

1. Excess. It isn't just politeness or respect. It is too much — over the top. A respectful employee completes their work well and treats their boss with courtesy. An obsequious employee agrees with everything the boss says, praises every decision, and constantly looks for opportunities to flatter them. The excess is what makes it uncomfortable to watch.

2. Insincerity. The obsequious person doesn't genuinely mean what they say or do. They aren't being helpful because they care — they're being helpful because they want something. Deep down, they may not even like or respect the person they're flattering. The whole performance is hollow.

3. A Power Imbalance. Obsequious behaviour is almost always directed upward — toward someone with more power, status, wealth, or authority. A student might be obsequious toward a professor. An employee toward a CEO. A courtier toward a king. The obsequious person sees an advantage to gain by winning the approval of someone above them.

Obsequious is a negative word. When you call someone obsequious, you are criticising them. You are saying they are a people-pleaser in the worst sense — spineless, servile, and fake. It carries a strong flavour of contempt.

People who are obsequious are often called "yes-men" (or "yes-women") — they just agree with whoever is in charge rather than speaking honestly.

It is very different from saying someone is:

  • Polite — that's genuine, socially appropriate courtesy.
  • Respectful — that's sincere acknowledgment of someone's worth.
  • Helpful — that's caring about someone without a hidden agenda.

None of those words carry the uncomfortable, fake, self-serving quality that obsequious does.
Real-Life Examples to Make It Stick

Scenario 1: A manager makes a decision that half the team thinks is a bad idea. Most people stay quiet. But one person says, "Wow, that's such a sharp strategy — I was thinking the exact same thing!" They weren't. They just want to look good. That's obsequious.

Scenario 2: A politician always laughs at the president's jokes, mirrors their opinions, and finds a way to publicly praise them at every opportunity — not out of genuine admiration, but to stay in favour. Obsequious.

Scenario 3: A salesperson at a luxury store treats a visibly wealthy customer with exaggerated warmth, compliments their every choice, and agrees with everything they say — purely to close the sale. Obsequious.

• His obsequious manner in front of the director made his colleagues cringe.
  • She was obsequious toward anyone who could help her career, but cold to everyone else.
  • The obsequious assistant nodded vigorously at everything his boss said, even when it made no sense.
  • Don't be obsequious — speak your mind honestly, even if it's not what people want to hear.

The noun most closely linked to this adjective is sycophant — a person who is obsequious. If someone behaves in an obsequious way, you can call them a sycophant. The two words are a natural pair, and knowing both reinforces your understanding of each.

Obsequious means being fawningly eager to please someone powerful — not out of genuine respect or kindness, but out of self-interest — in a way that is excessive, insincere, and ultimately a little shameful to witness.
11253:
Observant describes someone who is very good at noticing things — things that many others would miss, overlook, or simply never register. An observant person keeps their eyes, ears, and mind actively open. They pay careful, sharp attention to their surroundings, to people, to details, and to small changes.

Think of a detective who walks into a room and immediately notices that a window is slightly open, there's a faint smell of coffee, and a chair has been moved. Most people would walk in and just see "a room." The detective sees everything in it. That detective is observant.
Meaning 1 — Noticing Things (The Most Common Use)

When someone is called observant, it usually means they have a sharp, alert awareness of what is happening around them. They pick up on small details, subtle shifts, and things that are easy to miss.

A doctor who notices that a patient's skin color has slightly changed, even before the patient says anything, is being observant. A teacher who sees that a usually cheerful student is unusually quiet today is being observant. A friend who remembers you briefly mentioned a preference months ago — and acts on it — is being observant.

Crucially, being observant is not just about looking — it's about actively noticing, processing, and registering what you see, hear, or sense. It is an active, engaged quality, not a passive one. You can stare directly at something and still fail to be observant if your mind isn't engaged.

This is also an inherently positive word. Calling someone observant is a compliment. It suggests they are switched-on, tuned-in, and aware in a way that is valuable.
Meaning 2 — Carefully Following Rules or Practices (Especially Religious Ones)

Observant has a second, completely distinct meaning. When someone is described as observant in a religious or cultural context, it means they faithfully and carefully follow the rules, rituals, and practices of their religion or tradition — not loosely or occasionally, but consistently and with commitment.

An observant Muslim prays five times daily and follows dietary rules. An observant Jew keeps the Sabbath, eats only kosher food, and attends synagogue. An observant Catholic attends Mass regularly and lives by Church teaching.

In this sense, they observe — meaning they honor, keep, and abide by — the laws of their faith. You will almost always see this meaning paired with a religious identity: "a deeply observant Sikh," "a moderately observant Christian," and so on.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings share the same underlying idea: paying close and faithful attention, and acting accordingly.

In Meaning 1, you pay close attention to the world around you and notice what others miss.
In Meaning 2, you pay close attention to the teachings of your faith and live by them.

In both cases, the person is not careless or inattentive — they are consciously and actively engaged.

Sharpening what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

Observant does not mean simply "watching." You can stare at something for an hour and still be completely unobservant if you're not registering its details.

It does not mean "nosy" or "intrusive." A nosy person pries into others' private affairs uninvited. An observant person simply notices things. The word carries no negative judgment.

It does not mean "intelligent." A brilliant person can be remarkably unobservant, and a person of average intellect can be extraordinarily observant. They are separate qualities. Observant is about awareness, not raw intelligence.

It does not mean "suspicious" or "paranoid." Those words carry a sense of mistrust. Observant is neutral and positive — it simply means noticing what is there.

Observant is not a yes-or-no quality. It exists on a spectrum, and it can also be specific to a domain.

A forensic scientist may be highly observant about physical evidence but completely miss that a colleague is upset. A chef may be observant about flavors and smells but not particularly about body language. A skilled nurse may be deeply observant about physical symptoms in patients. Context matters.
Similar Words — and How They Differ

Understanding nearby words helps you see the precise edges of a word's meaning.

Attentive means paying careful attention, but usually in a specific moment or toward a specific person ("an attentive listener"). Observant is broader — it describes a general, ongoing quality of awareness.

Perceptive means not only noticing things but also deeply understanding them, especially about emotions, people, or complex situations. Perceptive goes further inward. Observant is more about the noticing itself.

Alert means watchful and ready to respond, often with a sense of urgency or danger. Observant is calmer and more about detail than readiness.

Vigilant means carefully watching for threats or problems — it carries a more serious, guarded tone than observant.

Eagle-eyed is an informal expression meaning someone can spot very fine visual details, like an eagle spotting a mouse from high in the sky. It's close to observant but specifically about vision and precision.

Unobservant — the direct opposite; someone who fails to notice things around them.
Oblivious — completely unaware of what is happening.
Inattentive — not paying attention.
Absent-minded — so lost in thought that surroundings go unnoticed.
Heedless — not paying attention, often carelessly or recklessly.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

Observant can sit before a noun ("an observant child," "an observant scientist") or after a linking verb like is, was, seems ("she is very observant," "he was always observant"). It can be intensified with words like very, highly, deeply, remarkably, surprisingly, and keenly.

Some natural examples:

  • "Children are surprisingly observant — they notice everything adults do."
  • "You'd make a great doctor; you're very observant."
  • "She comes from a deeply observant Jewish family."
  • "His observant eye caught the tiny crack in the structure that everyone else had walked past."
  • "Being observant is one of the most valuable skills a nurse can have."

If you had to boil it down: observant means alert and sharp enough to notice what others miss — or, in a religious context, faithfully following the rules and practices of one's faith. In both cases, the person is actively and carefully paying attention to what matters.
11254: Observation refers to the act of carefully watching or noticing something — and it can also mean the remark or comment you make as a result of that noticing. The word carries a few closely related meanings, and understanding all of them will give you the complete picture.
Meaning 1: The act of watching or noticing with attention

This is the most fundamental meaning. Observation is not passive, absent-minded glancing. It means directing your genuine attention at something — using your eyes, ears, or other senses to actually take it in.

"His observation of the birds lasted for two hours."
"Her sharp observation skills helped her notice things others missed."

The key idea: you are not just looking — you are really seeing, picking up details, and staying alert.
Meaning 2: A remark or comment based on something you noticed

When you pay attention to something and then say something about it, that remark is called an observation. This is the most everyday use of the word in spoken and written English.

"She made an interesting observation about how people behave in traffic."
"His quiet observation was: 'The room feels different today.'"

The key idea: an observation, in this sense, is a comment grounded in what you actually noticed — not in imagination or pure feeling. This is why it sits closer to fact than to opinion. When someone says "that's just your opinion," they mean it's based on personal feeling. But when someone says "that's a fair observation," they mean it's based on something real and noticeable.
Meaning 3: Systematic watching to gather knowledge (scientific and formal use)

In science, medicine, and research, observation means carefully watching and recording something over time in order to understand it or draw conclusions from it.

"The scientists documented their observations over six months."
"Close observation of the patient showed signs of improvement."

The key idea: this is structured, intentional watching with a purpose. You're not just noticing — you're collecting information. Scientists call this "empirical observation," meaning knowledge gained directly through the senses rather than through theory alone.
Meaning 4: The state of being watched or monitored

Observation can also describe the condition of being under watch — usually in a medical or security context.

"The patient was kept under observation overnight."
"The suspect was placed under police observation."

The key idea: here, the word shifts from describing the watcher's action to describing the watched person's situation. Being "under observation" means someone is actively monitoring you.

Every meaning shares the same soul: deliberate, focused attention directed at something. Whether you're studying stars, commenting on something you noticed, running an experiment, or monitoring a patient — you are directing careful, conscious attention. That is what observation always means, at every level.
Observation vs. Opinion — an important distinction

These two are often confused.

  • An opinion comes from your personal feelings, values, or beliefs.
  • An observation comes from what you actually noticed with your senses or attention.

"This painting is beautiful." → Opinion (personal feeling)
"This painting uses mostly dark colors." → Observation (what you can directly see)

Observations can be verified — another person can look and check. Opinions cannot, because they live inside you.
Observation vs. Inference — another crucial distinction

This one matters especially in science and logic.

  • An observation is what you directly notice.
  • An inference is the conclusion you draw from that observation.

"The pavement is wet." → Observation (you can see it)
"It must have rained." → Inference (you're reasoning about a cause)

Keeping these two separate is important: an observation reports what is, while an inference interprets why or how.

• Make an observation — to say something you've noticed
  • Under observation — being monitored or watched
  • Close/careful observation — paying very focused attention
  • Keen observation — sharp, insightful noticing; catching what others miss
  • Direct observation — watching something firsthand, not through a report
  • Observational skills — the ability to notice things accurately and in detail
  • Powers of observation — the same idea, used more idiomatically
One final nuance: tone and social use

When someone begins a sentence with "I have an observation...", they're signaling: "I noticed something worth pointing out." It sounds measured and thoughtful — more grounded than starting with "I think..." or "In my opinion..." It implies the speaker is reporting from the world, not just from their own head.

This is also why skilled writers, scientists, detectives, and doctors are praised for their "powers of observation" — the ability to notice what others overlook, and to report it accurately, is considered a sign of intelligence and care.
11255: An observatory is a place — usually a building or a facility — specially built and equipped for observing and studying things that are far away, most commonly objects in the sky like stars, planets, the Moon, and galaxies. Think of it as a scientific "watching station."

The word captures two things at once: a place and a purpose. The purpose is systematic, careful observation — not just glancing at the sky casually, but studying it in a precise, organized, and repeatable way. The place is designed entirely around making that observation as accurate and powerful as possible.
What You'll Find Inside (or Around) an Observatory

The most iconic feature is the telescope — often a very large one, far more powerful than anything an ordinary person owns. The building that houses it usually has a dome-shaped roof with a slit or opening that can be aimed at different parts of the sky. The dome can rotate so the telescope can point in any direction.

Alongside the telescope, you'll typically find:

  • Cameras and sensors attached to the telescope to capture images or data
  • Computers to record, store, and analyze what is observed
  • Clocks and timing instruments, because precise time-keeping is critical in astronomy
  • Control rooms where scientists operate the equipment

While astronomical observatories (for studying space) are the most common type people think of, the word "observatory" has a broader meaning. Any facility built for systematic, scientific watching can be called an observatory. This includes:

  • Meteorological observatories — for watching and recording weather patterns (temperature, wind, rainfall, atmospheric pressure)
  • Seismic observatories — for monitoring earthquakes and ground movements
  • Solar observatories — dedicated specifically to studying the Sun (its surface, flares, sunspots)
  • Radio observatories — which don't use visible light at all, but instead pick up radio waves from space using large dish-shaped antennas

What they all share is the same principle: a fixed, well-equipped location devoted entirely to careful, long-term watching and measurement.

You might wonder: why can't scientists just use a telescope anywhere? The answer is that observatories are built in very specific locations for good reasons:

  • High altitude — Mountain-top observatories sit above much of the atmosphere, which distorts light. Less atmosphere means sharper, clearer images.
  • Dry climate — Clouds and humidity ruin observations, so many observatories are built in deserts or arid regions.
  • Far from city lights — Light pollution from cities washes out faint stars. Remote locations give astronomers dark skies.
  • Stable ground — Especially for earthquake-monitoring observatories, a location with stable geological conditions matters a great deal.

Famous examples include the Mauna Kea Observatories in Hawaii (perched atop a dormant volcano), the Palomar Observatory in California, and the Jodrell Bank Observatory in England (a radio observatory).

Primarily scientists and researchers — astronomers, astrophysicists, meteorologists, and geologists, depending on the type. However, many observatories also welcome the general public for educational visits and stargazing nights, making them places of learning as well as research.

Some observatories are run by universities, others by government agencies (like NASA), and some by private organizations.

In modern usage, the word has also extended to space-based observatories — telescopes and instruments launched into orbit around Earth. The Hubble Space Telescope is one famous example. Being in space removes all atmospheric interference entirely, allowing observations of extraordinary clarity. These are still called observatories because they serve the exact same purpose: systematic, scientific observation — just from a platform above Earth's atmosphere.

An observatory represents humanity's organized effort to look beyond what our naked eyes can see and gather reliable knowledge about the universe (or Earth itself). It is more than just a building with a big telescope — it is a scientific institution whose entire design, location, and equipment exist for one purpose: to see, measure, and understand.
11256: To obsess means to think about something — or someone — so constantly, so intensely, and so uncontrollably that it takes over your mind. The defining feature isn't just that you think about something a lot. It's that you can't stop, even when you try. The thought keeps returning on its own.
What Makes It Different from Simply "Thinking About Something"

Consider this scale:

Think about → Care about → Love → Be passionate about → Obsess

Each step is more intense than the last. "Obsess" sits at the extreme end. When you obsess over something, the thought doesn't stay neatly in its place — it bleeds into everything else. You're at dinner, but your mind is on that thing. You're trying to sleep, but that thought won't leave. That inability to switch off is the heart of the word.

1. Someone obsesses over / about something

This is the active form. The person is the one whose mind has been taken over.

  • She obsesses over every tiny detail of her work.
  • He obsesses about what people think of him.
  • They obsess over money constantly.

"Over" and "about" are both correct here and nearly interchangeable. "Over" feels slightly more intense in most contexts; "about" feels a bit more casual — but both work fine.

2. Someone is obsessed with / by something (most common)

This is the passive form, and it's the most frequently used construction in everyday English.

  • She is obsessed with true crime podcasts.
  • He was obsessed with becoming the best in his field.
  • They are completely obsessed by the idea of moving abroad.

"Obsessed with" is far more common in casual speech. "Obsessed by" has a slightly more formal or literary flavor but means the same thing. Both are correct.

3. Something obsesses someone (less common, but correct)

Here, the thing is the subject — it's doing the obsessing to the person. You'll see this more in writing than in speech.

  • The unanswered question obsessed him for years.
  • Fear of failure obsesses her.
  • One image from that day obsessed the artist throughout his life.

This pattern emphasizes that the person has no control — the thought acts upon them, rather than the other way around.
The Tone: Negative, Neutral, or Positive?

Traditionally, "obsess" carries a slightly negative or cautionary weight. It suggests that something is occupying more mental space than it should — often to the point of being unhealthy, harmful to relationships, or interfering with normal life.

  • He was so obsessed with his career that he ignored his family.
  • Her obsession with perfection made her miserable.

In modern informal usage, however — especially in conversation and on social media — "obsess" and "obsessed" are frequently used in a purely enthusiastic, positive way. The "can't stop thinking about it" quality remains, but the negative edge is dropped.

  • I am completely obsessed with this new café.
  • She's been obsessing over that album all week. (= she loves it and can't stop listening)
  • We are obsessed — this show is incredible.

Context will almost always make the meaning clear.
The Important Nuance: It Implies a Lack of Control

This is what separates obsess from words like love, enjoy, or even be passionate about. When you are passionate about something, you are in control — you choose to dedicate energy to it. When you obsess, the thought has power over you. It demands your attention whether or not you give it permission.

This is also why "obsess" is used in psychology to describe intrusive, unwanted thought patterns. The clinical condition OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) gets its name from this same root idea.

• Think about → neutral, no intensity, fully in control
  • Worry about → negative focus, but manageable
  • Be passionate about → positive and controlled dedication
  • Be fixated on → close to "obsess," but more clinical and detached in tone
  • Obsess → extreme, persistent, uncontrollable — can be joyfully positive (informal) or seriously negative depending on context
A Few Natural Examples Across Different Contexts

• Stop obsessing over things you can't control. (advice to let go)
  • She has been obsessed with astronomy since she was twelve. (a deep, long-standing passion)
  • He obsessed about the argument for days, replaying every word. (anxious, unwanted rumination)
  • The whole team is obsessed with winning this year. (intense focus — could be admirable or excessive)
  • I'm obsessed with this recipe, I've made it five times this month. (casual, enthusiastic love)
To obsess is to be held captive by a thought or feeling — to think about something so relentlessly and uncontrollably that it dominates your mind, whether you want it to or not.
11257:
When someone is obsessed with something or someone, it means that thing has taken over their mind. They think about it constantly, almost without being able to stop — even when they don't want to, even when it's inconvenient, even when there are other things they should be focusing on. The thought keeps coming back, again and again, like a song stuck in your head, except far more powerful and harder to shake off.

The key idea is loss of mental control. A person who is merely very interested in something can choose to stop thinking about it and move on. An obsessed person struggles to do that. Their mind returns to the subject on its own.
What It Feels Like From the Inside

Imagine you just had a big argument with a friend. Even hours later — while eating, while watching TV, while trying to sleep — your mind keeps replaying what was said. You can't stop thinking about it. That pull, that involuntary, repeated return to one thing, is exactly the feeling that "obsessed" describes.

Now extend that to weeks, months, or even years, and apply it to any subject — a person, a hobby, a fear, an idea — and you have obsession.
The Spectrum: How Strong Can It Get?

"Obsessed" covers a wide range of intensity.

At the milder end, someone might say they're obsessed with a TV show. They binge-watch it, think about the characters often, and keep recommending it to others. It's intense interest — more than normal, but not harmful.

At the stronger end, the word describes something much darker. A person might be obsessed with an ex-partner and unable to move on with their life. They check the person's social media constantly, think about them all day, and feel a deep discomfort they can't escape. This kind of obsession can be emotionally destructive.

At the extreme end — which is the word's original, clinical meaning — obsession is a symptom of a psychological condition. A person might be obsessed with fear of germs, checking whether they locked the door, or counting things compulsively. Here, the person is trapped by their own mind; they know the thoughts are irrational but cannot stop them.
Positive vs. Negative? It Depends on Context

"Obsessed" is not always negative. Its connotation depends entirely on the context and tone.

Informal and positive use — In everyday, casual speech (especially among younger people), "obsessed" is used enthusiastically and lightly:

  • "I am absolutely obsessed with this song right now." — This just means they love it deeply and can't stop listening.
  • "Have you tried that new restaurant? I'm obsessed." — Strong enthusiasm, nothing alarming.

Here, "obsessed" is almost like a superlative: more than just liking, more than loving — intensely, constantly hooked.

Neutral to negative use — When used more seriously, the word signals a problem. It implies that the attachment is unhealthy, excessive, or interfering with normal life:

  • "He's obsessed with what people think of him." — He worries about it too much; it's harming him.
  • "She became obsessed with tracking his every move." — Clearly alarming behavior.

Clinical/psychological use — In formal or medical contexts, "obsessed" and "obsession" refer specifically to intrusive, unwanted, recurring thoughts that a person cannot control, often associated with conditions like OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder).

Understanding a word also means knowing what it doesn't mean — its boundaries.

FeelingDifference from "obsessed"

Interested — You think about something when it's relevant, but your mind doesn't chase it on its own. You are in control. An obsessed person is not.

Passionate — You love something deeply and dedicate real energy to it. But passion is healthy, productive, and chosen. Obsession is involuntary and often excessive or damaging.

Enthusiastic — You feel strong positive energy about something. But enthusiasm is a mood; obsession is a state that persists even in moods you'd rather be feeling.

Fixated — This word is close in meaning to obsessed and is often used interchangeably. "Fixated" slightly emphasizes the stuckness — being locked onto one point and unable to move away — while "obsessed" emphasizes the mental preoccupation. In practice, both are used very similarly.

The line between passion and obsession is this: passion energizes you; obsession consumes you.

"Obsessed" is an adjective. It always describes a person (or, less commonly, a group of people). It is not used to describe objects.

It almost always appears in one of these patterns:

"obsessed with" + noun/gerund — This is the most common pattern.

  • She is obsessed with cleanliness.
  • He's obsessed with winning.
  • They were obsessed with the idea of becoming famous.

"obsessed by" + noun — Less common but also correct. Often used in more formal writing.

  • He was obsessed by a fear he couldn't name.
  • She was obsessed by thoughts of failure.

Note: "obsessed with" is far more common in everyday usage. "Obsessed by" tends to appear in literary or formal writing and often implies the person feels somewhat passive — like something external is gripping them.

As a predicate adjective (after "be"):

  • He is obsessed. (alone, without "with" — this works and means his obsessive state is already clear from context)

Before a noun (attributive position) — Less common:

  • an obsessed fan — possible, but less typical than "a fan who is obsessed"

Casual and positive:

  • "I've been obsessed with this recipe ever since I tried it last week."
  • "Warning: once you start this game, you will become obsessed."

Mildly negative — excessive, but not alarming:

  • "She's a little obsessed with her grades; she checks the portal ten times a day."
  • "He's obsessed with being on time — if you're even one minute late, he gets anxious."

Clearly negative — unhealthy:

  • "After the breakup, he became obsessed with her. He couldn't eat, couldn't sleep, couldn't think about anything else."
  • "She was obsessed with the idea that people were judging her."

Clinical/psychological:

  • "The patient was obsessed with contamination and washed his hands over a hundred times a day."

These words share the same root and are essential to know alongside "obsessed":

To obsess (verb) — to dominate someone's mind, or to think about something constantly.

  • "Why do you obsess over things you can't control?"
  • "The problem obsessed him for years."

Obsession (noun) — the state of being obsessed; also, the specific thing someone is obsessed with.

  • "His obsession with success ruined his relationships."
  • "Football is a national obsession in this country." (Here it's used more lightly — a widely shared, intense passion.)

Obsessive (adjective) — describes a person prone to obsessing, or behavior that is characteristic of obsession; also used as a noun for such a person.

  • "She has an obsessive personality — she gives 100% to everything, sometimes too much."
  • "His obsessive attention to detail makes him a great editor." (Can be positive.)
  • "Obsessive thoughts kept him awake at night."

Obsessively (adverb) — in a way that shows obsession.

  • "She checked her phone obsessively throughout the day."
  • "He trained obsessively, sometimes forgetting to eat."

If you want one image to carry with you: think of a hamster wheel in the mind. The person is the hamster. The subject of their obsession is the wheel. The hamster keeps running — not always because it wants to, but because the wheel is always there and always spinning. That relentless, circular, hard-to-stop movement of thought is what "obsessed" captures.

It is one of those words that lives at the edge between love and suffering — because to be truly obsessed is to be fully captured by something, and whether that feels good or terrible depends entirely on what has captured you, and whether you can ever let it go.
11258:
An obsession is a thought, idea, feeling, image, or desire about a particular person, thing, or subject that keeps returning to your mind repeatedly, is very hard to control or stop, and takes up far more mental space than is normal.

Think of it this way: most thoughts come and go. You think about what to eat, you move on. But an obsessive thought is different — it comes back again and again, almost like a song stuck in your head, except you can't just choose to stop thinking about it. It dominates your attention.

The word "obsession" is used in two overlapping ways:

1. The everyday, informal meaning

In everyday speech, people use "obsession" to describe an extremely intense, consuming interest in or focus on something — often beyond what most people would consider normal.

  • "She has an obsession with true crime podcasts."
  • "His obsession with football means he watches every game, studies every statistic, and talks about it constantly."

In this sense, the word doesn't necessarily carry a negative feeling. Sometimes it's used almost proudly — "I'm obsessed with this band." The key idea is: it's an interest so intense that it takes over your thoughts more than a regular interest would.

2. The psychological meaning

In psychology and mental health, an obsession has a more specific and serious meaning. Here, it refers to an unwanted, intrusive thought or mental image that forces itself into your mind repeatedly, even though you don't want it there and you find it distressing.

For example, a person might keep having a thought like "Did I leave the stove on?" or "What if I hurt someone by accident?" — even after they've checked or know the thought is irrational. They didn't choose to think it; it just keeps arriving. This causes anxiety, not pleasure.

This psychological kind of obsession is a central feature of a condition called OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder), where obsessive thoughts are followed by compulsive actions meant to relieve the resulting anxiety.

Whether you use the word in the everyday sense or the clinical sense, an obsession always has these qualities:

  • It is persistent — it comes back repeatedly, not just once.
  • It is difficult or impossible to stop — the person cannot simply decide to stop thinking about it, no matter how hard they try.
  • It is consuming — it takes up a disproportionately large share of a person's attention and mental energy.
  • It often feels involuntary — the thought or urge arrives on its own, without being invited.
What obsession feels like from the inside

Imagine you're trying to focus on work, but your mind keeps drifting to the same thought — maybe a person, a worry, a goal, or a memory. You push it away. It comes back in a minute. You push it away again. It returns again. Eventually, you stop fighting it; it's just always there in the background (or the foreground) of your mind.

In the positive everyday sense, this can feel exciting and motivating — like a passion that won't let you rest.

In the clinical or more negative sense, it can feel exhausting, frightening, or deeply uncomfortable — like your own mind is working against you.
The spectrum from mild to severe

Obsession is not binary — it exists on a spectrum:

Mild interest → Enthusiasm → Passion → Deep fascination → Preoccupation → Fixation → Obsession

As you move along this spectrum, the thought becomes harder to control, more frequent, more consuming, and more likely to interfere with normal life.

A person who's mildly interested in cooking thinks about it sometimes. A person who's passionate about cooking thinks about it a lot and it brings them joy. A person obsessed with cooking cannot stop thinking about it, it dominates their conversations, their free time, their decisions — possibly at the expense of other parts of their life.

Yes, in the informal sense, obsession can absolutely be a positive or neutral thing. Many great artists, scientists, athletes, and entrepreneurs have been described as "obsessed" with their craft — meaning they devoted every waking moment to it with an almost uncontrollable drive. In this light, obsession is what separates the truly exceptional from the merely talented. It's the engine behind extraordinary achievement.

However, even a positive obsession can become harmful if it starts to damage your health, relationships, or overall life balance.
How it differs from similar words

These words are often confused with "obsession":

Passion — A very strong and deep interest in something. A passion feels chosen, joyful, and within your control. An obsession, by contrast, feels more like it has a grip on you — less in your control, more consuming.

Addiction — A strong, often physical or psychological dependence on a substance or behavior. Addiction is about craving and dependency. An obsession is primarily about thought — it lives in the mind first.

Compulsion — The urge to do something repeatedly. An obsession is the thought; a compulsion is the action that follows from it. Someone obsessed with germs (thought) may feel compelled to wash their hands repeatedly (action).

Fixation — Very similar to obsession; being mentally "stuck" on something. Often used interchangeably, but "fixation" tends to imply that your development or thinking has gotten stuck at one point, like a record skipping.

Preoccupation — A lighter, milder version. Your mind is occupied with something, but you can still function normally. Think of preoccupation as a whisper and obsession as a shout.
Common ways the word is used

• "an obsession with" — This is the most common construction. ("He has an obsession with perfection.")
  • "become an obsession" — Describes how something gradually takes over. ("What started as a hobby became an obsession.")
  • "border on obsession" — Getting very close to obsessive territory. ("Her devotion to her work borders on obsession.")
  • "unhealthy obsession" — Explicitly signals the negative kind.
  • "secret obsession" — Something you're intensely focused on but don't openly admit.
  • "lifelong obsession" — Something that has consumed you for your entire life or a very long time.

• A detective who cannot stop thinking about an unsolved case, even years after it's been officially closed, has an obsession with solving it.
  • A teenager who plasters their walls with posters of a band, listens to only that band, learns everything about every member, and spends hours each day on fan forums — that band has become an obsession.
  • A person who is terrified of fires and keeps mentally replaying images of their house burning down, even though there's no real danger and they know it — that is the clinical kind of obsession.
  • A writer who thinks about their novel every single waking hour, cannot relax until the chapter is perfect, and dreams about their characters — their book has become an obsession.

An obsession is a thought, desire, or focus on a person, thing, or idea that is so powerful, so repetitive, and so hard to control that it dominates your mind far beyond what's normal — ranging from an unusually intense but harmless interest, all the way to a distressing, unwanted thought that you cannot escape.
11259: Obsessive describes something — a thought, a feeling, a behavior, or a person — that is driven by an unusually intense, persistent, and hard-to-control fixation on something. When something is obsessive, it goes far beyond normal interest or concern. It dominates the mind in a way that feels almost involuntary — like the mind keeps returning to something even when the person wants to stop.

Think of a normal interest first. You might like a TV show and think about it sometimes. That's healthy. Now imagine you can't stop thinking about that show — during meals, at work, before sleep, even in conversations about something else. It keeps pulling your attention back. That pulling force — that compulsive, uncontrollable return to one thing — is what obsessive captures.

The word is used in two main ways:

1. To describe thoughts or behaviors that won't let go
An obsessive thought is one that a person keeps having again and again, even when they try to push it away. It isn't invited — it just appears, repeatedly. An obsessive behavior is one driven by that kind of thought, like repeatedly checking whether a door is locked because the mind refuses to accept the answer.

2. To describe a person's personality or way of engaging with something
An obsessive person is someone who tends to fixate deeply and intensely. They don't just like things — they become consumed by them. They return to the same subject, object, or goal with relentless focus, often to a degree that seems excessive to others.

Several features are almost always present when something is truly obsessive:

  • Intensity — The interest or concern is extreme, not mild.
  • Persistence — It doesn't fade naturally. It keeps coming back.
  • Difficulty stopping — The person struggles to pull away, even when they want to.
  • Disproportionality — The amount of mental energy spent is far greater than the situation seems to call for.

This word can carry both negative and (mildly) positive meaning depending on context.

Negative: Most often, obsessive implies something unhealthy or excessive. An obsessive jealousy in a relationship is controlling and destructive. An obsessive worry about germs might stop someone from living normally. Here, the word suggests the person is not in full control of their own mind — the fixation is ruling them.

Neutral or even admiring: In casual, everyday use, people sometimes call a highly dedicated person obsessive with a hint of admiration. "She's obsessive about her craft" might mean she gives it extraordinary focus and refuses to settle for less than perfect. This usage is complimentary in tone, though it still carries the idea of going beyond ordinary dedication.

The difference comes from context: Is this fixation hurting the person or those around them? Is it disrupting normal life? If yes, the word is critical. If it's producing excellence and not causing harm, it might carry grudging respect.

You will often hear this word in connection with OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder). In this context, obsessive refers specifically to unwanted, intrusive thoughts that cause the person anxiety — thoughts they did not choose and cannot easily dismiss. These are not daydreams or fantasies; they are distressing, repetitive mental intrusions. The person knows the thought is irrational but still cannot make it stop. This is the most clinically precise use of the word.

However, you don't need to be diagnosed with anything for behavior or thinking to be called obsessive. The word is freely used in everyday life for any pattern of extreme, hard-to-break fixation.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Passionate — A passionate person loves something deeply and pursues it with energy. But they are still in control. Passion enriches life; obsession can take it over. Passionate is almost always positive. Obsessive is neutral to negative.
  • Dedicated / Committed — These suggest strong, steady focus chosen freely. An obsessive focus feels less chosen — it feels imposed on the person by their own mind.
  • Fixated — Very close to obsessive, but fixated often implies the mind is stuck on one point and unable to move on (like being fixated on a past failure). Obsessive more often implies a repetitive, cycling pattern of returning to something over and over.
  • Compulsive — While often used alongside obsessive, compulsive focuses more on the behavior — the driven, automatic urge to do something. Obsessive leans more toward the thought or feeling that drives it. You have obsessive thoughts; you perform compulsive actions.

• His obsessive attention to detail meant every page of the report was flawless, but it also meant he never finished anything on time.
  • She couldn't shake the obsessive thought that she had left the stove on, even though she had checked it three times.
  • Their obsessive rivalry had consumed both of them for years.
  • He became obsessive about his health after the diagnosis — tracking every meal, every step, every hour of sleep.
  • The film portrays an obsessive love that slowly turns into something dangerous.

If you want to remember this word simply: obsessive = when the mind grips something so tightly it can't easily let go, and that grip controls the person more than the person controls it. It's the difference between having a thought and being haunted by one. Between caring about something and being consumed by it.
